assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's demonstration of record accuracy and coherence, moved timekeeping to the 10^-18 level. This is a clear, original idea with large consequences for metrology, geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and the prospective redefinition of the second. It fits the principle that progress is limited by what can be measured and how accurately.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice trapping scheme and made early demonstrations; Ye's group brought the clocks to the accuracy and stability frontier. Two laureates give a clean configuration. Others (Lemke, Ludlow, Takamoto and the frequency-comb contributors) are not in the credited list, and I cannot independently verify every priority detail.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by many independent groups worldwide and mature for two decades; the interpretation is stable. Timing is good, although the SI second redefinition has not yet happened.
uncertainties: Overlap with the comb and ion-clock prizes (2005, 2012) may raise a question of incremental novelty.
Allocation between Katori and Ye versus other lattice-clock contributors is not fully settled in the supplied credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Realising Hubbard-model physics with ultracold atoms in optical lattices, including the superfluid to Mott insulator transition and fermionic Mott states, created quantum simulation as an experimental discipline. Originality, clarity and lasting impact are all high, and the work links atomic physics to condensed-matter questions.
assessment.attribution: Theory (Jaksch and Zoller; Cirac) was decisive for the proposals, and Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger carried the experimental realisations; I chose the experimental trio. Five credited names exceed the three-laureate limit, so Cirac and Zoller, who are also credited in B061, would be left out. That is a real allocation tension. Greiner's role relative to Bloch's group in the 2002 work should be examined.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced widely, now with quantum gas microscopes and large-scale simulators. Mature and stable.
uncertainties: Exclusion of the key theorists is contentious.
Fairness of the three experimentalist subset is not certain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: BB84 and the entanglement-based E91 protocol founded quantum cryptography and made the quantum nature of information concrete. Conceptual originality is high, and the experimental realisations are in commercial and satellite use. The 2022 prize for entanglement experiments strengthens the context.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard are the BB84 originators, and Ekert proposed the entanglement-based protocol. The three credited names give a natural configuration, though Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea and later security proofs are outside the credited names.
assessment.maturity: Decades of experimental validation, field trials and satellite links. Mature, with security-proof questions on implementation largely resolved in principle.
uncertainties: Real-world device security and practical deployment are secondary to the foundational idea.
Wiesner's precursor credit may complicate priority.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED, with strong coupling of superconducting qubits to microwave resonators, provides the platform for readout, control and entanglement in superconducting quantum processors. High impact and a clean physical concept analogous to cavity QED, which I know well.
assessment.attribution: Blais supplied the theory proposal with Wallraff and Schoelkopf, and Wallraff and Schoelkopf's groups did the 2004 experiment with colleagues. The credited trio is a reasonable fit, although Devoret and Yale colleagues' contributions, and the 2025 prize for circuit macroscopic quantum effects, complicate how the field's credit is split.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed in many labs and now an industrial platform. Recognition would be timely, although a recent related prize slightly lowers urgency.
uncertainties: Credit division with Yale co-authors not specified in the supplied names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light for interferometry began with Caves's quantum-noise analysis and led to squeezed-vacuum injection in GEO600 and LIGO, improving sensitivity beyond classical limits. This is quantum optics directly improving a Nobel-recognised instrument.
assessment.attribution: Caves for the theoretical proposal, Kimble for early experimental squeezing, and Schnabel for the GEO600 and LIGO-relevant implementation. Mavalvala, Walls, Slusher, Vahlbruch and others are significant but beyond three names, so allocation is uncertain.
assessment.maturity: Operational in LIGO, Virgo and GEO600 since 2019, so confirmation is strong. The 2017 prize covers detection, so it is a different contribution.
uncertainties: Many contributors across theory, experiment and implementation make a three-name prize hard.
Kimble also appears in other candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Coherent atom-light interfaces, including single-atom cavity QED, photon-by-photon control and quantum memories, underpin quantum networks. This is close to my own work on optical quantum memories, so I weigh it with caution about my familiarity. The concept is important and still growing.
assessment.attribution: Rempe, Kimble and Lukin are leading, but this is a broad compound area. Rare-earth-ion memories, EIT-based storage and DLCZ repeaters involve other groups that are not credited, and I should not argue for work related to my own. Attribution is therefore unclear.
assessment.maturity: Many demonstrations, though practical repeaters have not yet been achieved. Maturity is moderate.
uncertainties: Breadth of the topic makes a sharp discovery hard to define.
My own field proximity may bias my view.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Aberration-corrected electron microscopy brought sub-angstrom resolution and routine atomic-resolution imaging in materials physics. It is a rare instrument invention with demonstrated lasting impact, comparable to past Nobel recognition of instrumentation.
assessment.attribution: Rose designed the corrector theory, while Haider and Urban built and demonstrated the corrected microscope. This three-way split matches the commonly cited history. Related contributions by Krivanek and others fall outside the credited list.
assessment.maturity: Commercially widespread and independently confirmed for twenty years. The recognition is already prominent and mature.
uncertainties: Krivanek and Dellby's parallel work is outside the credited names.
Whether committee considers this physics rather than instrumentation or chemistry is a question.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry makes matter-wave sensors for gravity, rotation and tests of fundamental physics. It is an original idea with broad precision-measurement reach, though its recognition may be partly covered by laser cooling and BEC prizes.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard realised early atom interferometers, Bordé developed the theory and the Ramsey-Bordé interferometer, and Kasevich showed gravimeters and gyroscopes. Chu, Hänsch, Mlynek and Müller also have important roles, and Chu is already a laureate. The three-name selection is therefore debatable.
assessment.maturity: Mature in gravimetry and in test-of-physics experiments; long-baseline and space instruments are still developing.
uncertainties: Priority and credit allocation are disputed among several groups.
Holger Müller's work is excluded by my choice of three names.
